newsitem.title: CROATIA: Tudjman's approval rating over 80 percent - survey.
newsitem.headline: Tudjman's approval rating over 80 percent - survey.

text.p: Four out of five Croatians approve President Franjo Tudjman's record so far, according to a survey despite growing economic discontent and charges the government is trying to muzzle the media, newspapers said on Thursday.

The poll carried out in late November by the United States Information Agency (USIA), showed that approval for Tudjman had risen to 81 percent up five percentage points since its last survey in February.

The finding was in marked contrast to that of Croatian sruveys, conducted at the same time, and Croatian analysts who say Tujdman's rating has fallen because of the deteriorating economy and a backlash against government curbs on the press.

A poll in the newspaper Globus on November 29 said only 31 per cent of Croats would support the 74-year-old Tudjman, who has reportedly been diagnosed as suffering terminal stomach cancer, if he contested presidential elections next year.
The USIA poll did not ask how Croats would vote.

The U.S. poll found that 81 percent of respondents approved of Tudjman, who led Croatia to independence from former Yugoslavia in 1991 where as Globus asked those polled whether they would vote for again for him again.
The USIA had 77 percent of people in Zagreb and other parts of Croatia saying they approved of Tudjman's performance.

Tudjman's popularity appeared unaffected by a mass protest in Zagreb in November when 100,000 people demonstrated against the government's attempt to shut down independent Radio 101, forcing the authorities to back down.
"Perhaps because the conflict over Radio 101 was resolved quickly, and due to concern over Tudjman's health, his popularity is apparently unshaken by the events in Zagreb," USIA said in a comment.
Its poll showed Tudjman enjoyed the overwhelming support of young town dwellers and the well educated, two groups thought to be the most critical of his autocratic ruling style.

Although his popularity among Zagreb residents, put at 66 percent, was significantly lower than the national average, 73 percent of those under 30 and 64 percent of those with a university education support the president.
The poll noted increased sensitivity to the issue of free media but the government crackdown did not seem to be directly linked with Tudjman.

The USIA said 88 percent of people support the development of private, commercial radio and TV stations. The number of those thinking that the national television and radio were biased grew to 72 percent from 64 percent in 1994.
Only one in four persons thought state radio reports and news were unbiased, while more than half of the population thought private radios dealt fairly with all sides.
